hook: Lead(II) chloride is fairly soluble in pure water for a "slightly soluble" salt, about four and a half grams per liter. Pour in some table salt, and almost all of that lead chloride falls out as a white solid. Nothing about lead chloride has changed. The solution simply already had one of its ions, and that changes the balance.

prereq.q: For PbCl<sub>2</sub>, what is the K<sub>sp</sub> expression?
prereq.why: Ion concentrations, each to its coefficient; the solid is left out.

prereq.q: Adding a product to a system at equilibrium makes it shift
prereq.why: Le Châtelier: it partly uses up what was added.

prereq.q: When should you check the small-x approximation?
prereq.why: The 5% check confirms the dropped term really is small.

figure.caption: More Cl<sup>−</sup> from NaCl means less PbCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves. K<sub>sp</sub> does not change; Q does.

chain.cause: A soluble salt adds an ion that is also in a solubility equilibrium

chain.effect: the slightly soluble salt precipitates until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>

chain.cause: The equilibrium is restored with the common ion present
chain.effect: less of the salt is dissolved: its molar solubility is lower
K<sub>sp</sub> is the same; only the solubility changed

ideas: The common-ion effect: an ion already in solution lowers the solubility of a salt that contains it.
Justify it with Q: the common ion raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>, so solid forms until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>. K<sub>sp</sub> does not change.
In calculations, the shared ion is (common ion + coefficient × s) ≈ common ion. Count ions per formula unit; check the 5% rule.
An ion that is squared in K<sub>sp</sub> has a larger effect.

misconception.wrong: Adding NaCl lowers the K<sub>sp</sub> of PbCl₂, so less dissolves.
misconception.right: K<sub>sp</sub> depends only on temperature. Added Cl⁻ raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>, so PbCl₂ precipitates until Q = K<sub>sp</sub>; the solubility falls, the constant does not.

summary: The common-ion effect: a salt is less soluble in a solution that already contains one of its ions. The common ion raises Q above K<sub>sp</sub>, so the salt precipitates until Q = K<sub>sp</sub> again; K<sub>sp</sub> is unchanged and only the solubility drops. To calculate the new solubility, write the shared ion as common ion plus a small term, drop the small term, solve K<sub>sp</sub> for s and check the 5% rule.
